Name: Codeforces
Notes: The centre of gravity for CP. Largest tagged problem bank, a rating system people actually optimise for, and `/edu/courses` is the only official course system on any judge. Editorials come from the setters, in the blog.

Name: AtCoder
Notes: The cleanest problem statements in CP and the best difficulty calibration. ABC A–D is the correct ramp below Codeforces 1600; ARC/AGC take over after.

Name: LeetCode
Notes: A different sport from CP — pattern recall in 25 minutes, no I/O tuning, no math depth. Paywalled parts: company tags and much of the solutions content. ⚠ URL shapes drift between redesigns; `leetcode.com` 403s automated clients.

Name: CSES Problem Set
Notes: ~300 problems, no filler, ordered by topic. The de-facto "am I ready for CF 1600" benchmark, and the only problem set with a matching free textbook.

Name: USACO
Notes: The official US olympiad ladder, and still the best difficulty ramp anywhere. ⚠ The legacy training pages are mid-migration: new usaco.org accounts are not recognised there and a separate legacy account is needed.

Name: CodeChef
Notes: India-heavy and underrated: the 10-day Long Challenge format teaches persistence and partial scoring in a way two-hour contests cannot. Its free `/learn` track is a genuine structured DSA course.

Name: DMOJ
Notes: The only large judge with an *editorial filter* in problem search. Carries CCC/CCO/IOI/COCI and a huge Canadian contest archive.

Name: Kattis
Notes: Huge bank, clean UI, and the judge most university algorithms courses actually use. Good for volume, thin on editorials.

Name: ICPC
Notes: The governing body: rules, regional structure, World Finals. For problems, use the archive or CF gyms — see Honest notes on the Live Archive.

Name: IOI
Notes: Read the Syllabus once. It is the only authoritative statement of what "competitive DSA" is scoped to include — and it is much narrower than most prep plans assume.

Name: oj.uz
Notes: The best English-language mirror of national olympiad and IOI problems, with subtask scoring preserved. Where you go when you want olympiad-style problems without Chinese or Polish.

Name: QOJ
Notes: Modern judge with a large gym of OI/ICPC problem sets. ⚠ Cloudflare-gated; automated checkers get an interstitial rather than the page.

Name: SPOJ
Notes: Enormous and old. Excellent for drilling a single technique to death; weak statements and uneven test data. ⚠ Canonical host is `spoj.com` — `spoj.pl` is a dead end, and the site 403s automated clients on some paths.

Name: UVa Online Judge
Notes: Thousands of classic problems, weak statements by modern standards. uHunt is the reason to bother: it gives UVa the topic-ladder structure the judge itself never had.

Name: Timus
Notes: A classic hard bank with deliberately unforgiving I/O. Good training for "the statement is one sentence and the edge cases are yours to find".

Name: ACMP
Notes: Russian olympiad-style archive, unusually good for high-volume beginner practice with tight time limits.

Name: beecrowd (URI)
Notes: Large beginner-friendly bank, strong in LATAM, English/Portuguese statements. Best used as warm-up volume, not for hard problems.

Name: Luogu
Notes: The largest problem set anywhere, Chinese statements. Worth it for the solution discussions if you can read them or use machine translation; otherwise a last resort.

Name: HDU
Notes: Massive Chinese archive with weak editorial culture. Use for volume on a specific tag.

Name: Nowcoder
Notes: Chinese contests plus campus/OA-style problem sets — useful if you want to see how Chinese placement exams are shaped.

Name: LightOJ
Notes: Topic-categorised bank, popular in South Asia. Some content sits behind an account.

Name: e-olymp
Notes: Multi-language training sets and school-level olympiad material. Broad, shallow.

Name: Toph
Notes: Bangladeshi judge with a genuinely good problem set and clean editorial support. ⚠ Returns 405 to automated HEAD checks; loads in a browser.

Name: CS Academy
Notes: Clean archive plus its own rounds. Small but well-curated; a nice change of pace.

Name: VJudge
Notes: Not a judge — a proxy. It pulls problems from other OJs so you can host your own virtual or mashup contest with teammates. Indispensable for team practice, useless as a source of truth.

Name: Library Checker
Notes: Submit your own segtree, NTT, flow or matroid-intersection implementation and have it machine-verified against ~200 known-hard cases. The fastest way to find the bug in a library you trusted.

Name: Project Euler
Notes: 1000+ problems that are half number theory, half implementation. The bridge between proofy math and code, and the strongest argument for learning modular arithmetic properly.

Name: USACO Guide
Documentation: https://usaco.guide/; https://usaco.guide/bronze; https://usaco.guide/silver; https://usaco.guide/gold; https://usaco.guide/plat; https://usaco.guide/adv
Notes: The fastest "I can code" → contest-ready path, and the only CP curriculum with per-division entry points. Start at your division, not the homepage. Platinum and `/adv` are thinner than Bronze–Gold.

Name: Competitive Programmer's Handbook
Notes: The one coherent free CP textbook. Chapters 21–24 (number theory, combinatorics, matrices, probability) are the only free CP-math treatment sized right. The published Springer version (*Guide to Competitive Programming*) adds chapters if you want more.

Name: CP3 book site (Halim & Halim)
Notes: The book is the standard reference for problem *taxonomy*; the site's topic index is free and is the best "what should I learn next" map after USACO Guide.

Name: cp-algorithms
Notes: The de-facto CP reference, and the successor to e-maxx — the project was renamed, so links to `e-maxx.ru` or `e-maxx-eng.github.io` are stale. Code-first and correct; weak on *why*.

Name: IOI Syllabus
Notes: The authoritative scope document for olympiad-level DSA, maintained by the ISC. Cross-check your prep plan against it: it excludes calculus, statistics and combinatorial game theory outright.

Name: Algorithms — Jeff Erickson
Notes: The best free *rigorous* algorithms textbook: recursion, backtracking, DP, greedy, graphs, flows, NP-hardness — plus hundreds of pages of extra lecture notes. Assumes discrete math and basic DS; not a first book. ⚠ The `algorithms.wtf` shortcut is dead.

Name: Open Data Structures
Notes: Free, complete, multi-language, and better written than most paid data-structure books. The proofs are short and the code is real.

Name: Algorithms, 4th Edition
Notes: Sedgewick/Wayne, used as a textbook in several IOI training camps. The booksite ships every implementation and the test data.

Name: Algorithm Design (Kleinberg & Tardos)
Notes: The clearest writing on algorithm *design* technique, with the best network-flow chapter of any textbook. ⚠ `kt.cs.princeton.edu` is dead — this is the working official page.

Name: The Algorithm Design Manual (Skiena)
Notes: Skiena's "catalogue of algorithmic problems" is the best shortcut in existence for the question "what standard problem is this, actually?".

Name: KACTL
Notes: ~25 pages that cover a World Finals toolkit. Read it as a checklist of things you should be able to implement.

Name: AtCoder Library
Notes: Official, maintained, and the reference implementation the whole community converges on. Read it before reimplementing a segment tree or modint, then beat it.

Name: OI Wiki
Notes: Deep, continuously updated, Chinese-first. ⚠ The English mirror at `oi-wiki.org/en/` 404s; use browser translation or USACO Guide instead.

Name: PEG Wiki
Notes: Older, unglamorous, and genuinely deep on CP-specific tricks. Better than Wikipedia for the things that only exist in contests.

Name: IMO official
Notes: The primary archive. Use it rather than a scraper; the results page lets you calibrate how hard a given year's P1 versus P3 actually was.

Name: AoPS Wiki
Notes: The reference corpus for competition math: theory pages plus per-year AMC/AIME/IMO/USAMO solutions. Free, community-maintained, uneven depth.

Name: AoPS Community
Notes: Where hard olympiad solutions actually get explained, usually three different ways, within a day of the contest. ⚠ 403s automated clients.

Name: AoPS Alcumus
Notes: Free adaptive math trainer with topic targeting. The single best free drill tool in this category — it does spaced repetition of *problem types*, which is exactly what contest training needs.

Name: TU Eindhoven IMO collection
Notes: One of the few organised collections of IMO **shortlists**, which — not the contests themselves — are the real training set at IMO level.

Name: Kalva
Notes: John Scholes' classic archive: IMO, USAMO and national olympiads with solutions alongside statements. Two independent mirrors exist for a reason — keep both.

Name: Evan Chen
Notes: The best free olympiad-math training index on the internet, from an IMO gold medallist. `Napkin` is the fastest route from "I know contest math" to "I can read the language real mathematicians use". ⚠ `web.evanchen.us` no longer resolves.

Name: Yufei Zhao
Notes: MIT faculty and a former olympiad medallist; his handouts (combinatorics, number theory, graph theory) are short, modern and pitched exactly at the olympiad/research boundary.

Name: MAA — AMC
Notes: Official home of AMC 8/10/12 — the entry rung of the US ladder. ⚠ Old `maa.org/math-competitions/*` paths now 404; these are the current ones.

Name: MAA — invitational competitions
Notes: AIME, USAMO and USAJMO — the invitation-only tiers. Past papers here, discussion on AoPS.

Name: MAA — Putnam archive
Notes: This is the official archive — the one that used to be awkward to find. The premier undergraduate exam in North America; median score is frequently zero, which tells you how to use it.

Name: Kedlaya's Putnam archive
Notes: Long-standing mirror covering older years, results and winner lists the official archive does not surface as conveniently. Keep it alongside the MAA one.

Name: USAMTS
Notes: Free, proof-graded, by-mail US contest with generous deadlines. Rare and valuable: full-solution grading by a human is the only way to learn to write proofs.

Name: UKMT
Notes: The UK ladder (Junior/Senior/BMO). Its mentoring scheme and past papers are high quality and less saturated than AoPS material.

Name: IMC
Notes: International Mathematics Competition for University Students. Problems and solutions free; a good step up from olympiad geometry into analysis-flavoured contest math.

Name: AwesomeMath
Notes: Summer camps plus a book line by olympiad coaches, several of them former IMO team leaders. The books are the reason it is indexed here — they sit between AoPS's introductory texts and research-level problem books.

Name: HBCSE Olympiads (India)
Notes: The official Indian olympiad programme: PRMO, RMO, INMO and the IMOTC. If you are in India this is the actual pipeline, and its past papers are the realistic difficulty reference — not AoPS highlight reels.

Name: MATHCOUNTS
Notes: The US middle-school competition pipeline. Only relevant if you are starting from a weak math base — but if you are, it is the correct rung to start on rather than jumping to AMC 10.

Name: OEIS
Notes: Turns "1, 2, 6, 22, 101…" into a closed form, recurrence, generating function and citations. On CP problems with a combinatorial flavour this is close to an unfair advantage.

Name: generatingfunctionology (Wilf)
Notes: The best single source for generating functions once combinatorics starts hurting; the enumerative tool CP counting problems quietly assume. ⚠ I could not confirm a durable direct PDF URL — the UPenn pages block automated clients. Use the catalogue record above, or search `Wilf generatingfunctionology pdf site:upenn.edu`.

Name: Shoup — A Computational Introduction to Number Theory and Algebra
Notes: The only number-theory-and-algebra book written for people who will implement the algorithms. Free from the author, rigorous, and it covers modular arithmetic properly — which almost no CP resource does.

Name: clist.by
Notes: The only reliable single calendar for Codeforces, AtCoder, CodeChef and ICPC mirrors, in your timezone, plus a cross-judge problem search. ⚠ `clist.by/api/` (bare) 404s — the docs path above is the working one.

Name: Codeforces API
Notes: Unofficial and undocumented in places, but stable for a decade. The only way to build your own rating tracker or problem recommender without scraping HTML.

Name: AtCoder Problems (kenkoooo)
Notes: Difficulty-coloured AtCoder problem browser, progress tracking and virtual-contest generation. The single best per-judge analytics tool in CP.

Name: online-judge-tools/oj
Notes: Submit, download samples and run local tests from the command line across Codeforces, AtCoder, AOJ and more. Once you use it, browser submission feels like a regression.

Name: cf-tool
Notes: Codeforces from the terminal: parse, generate, submit, watch verdicts. Pairs with competitive-companion.

Name: competitive-companion
Notes: Browser extension that hands a problem — statement, samples, limits — straight to your editor. The missing link between reading a problem and writing code.

Name: atcoder-cli
Notes: Scaffold and submit AtCoder contests locally. Two tools, same job, different ergonomics — try both.

Name: testlib
Notes: `testlib.h`, by Codeforces' author — the standard checker/generator/validator library. If you ever host a contest or generate stress tests, this is what the ecosystem uses.

Name: Library Checker problems
Notes: A ~200-problem verification suite for algorithm libraries. Wire it into CI and your template stops rotting.

Name: DMOJ judge server
Notes: Two production-quality open-source judges. Self-host one if you want full control over time limits, checkers and scoring — or just to understand what a judge actually does.

Name: Compiler Explorer
Notes: Read the assembly your solution actually compiles to. The fastest cure for cargo-cult "optimisation" in hot loops.

Name: cppreference
Notes: The C++ standard's readable form. ⚠ 403s automated clients; loads fine in a browser.

Name: StopStalk
Notes: Cross-judge activity tracker, popular in India: aggregates solves and ratings across Codeforces, CodeChef, SPOJ, HackerRank and more.

Name: Nayuki — fast Fibonacci algorithms
Notes: The clearest treatment of fast doubling and matrix methods for linear recurrences, with proofs and implementations. The reference to reach for before implementing Berlekamp–Massey or Bostan–Mori.

Name: Chess Programming Wiki
Notes: Not a chess resource in this context — it is the best free writing on hashing, transposition tables, bitboards and adversarial search anywhere. Directly transferable to CP game and search problems.

Name: Apache DataSketches
Notes: Production-grade probabilistic data structures (HyperLogLog, theta sketches, quantiles). Read it when CP's toy sketches meet real cardinality-estimation requirements.

Name: Sorting implementations
Notes: pdqsort is what libstdc++ and Rust now ship; PBBS is the parallel-algorithms benchmark suite. The fastest way to learn what "fast sort" means after 2015. See the [pdqsort paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.05123).

Name: Complexity Zoo
Notes: The catalogue of complexity classes. Use it to stop hand-waving about NP-hardness in interviews.

Name: LeetCode (company / premium)
Notes: The company-tag filters are **Premium**. Most "company-wise preparation" advice silently assumes you have it; if you do not, the free substitutes below are the fallback.

Name: HackerRank
Notes: Clean statements and easy filters; a good warm-up venue. ⚠ The contest product has been shrinking — ProjectEuler+ still loads but is login-gated.

Name: CodeSignal
Notes: CodeSignal is a real OA vendor, and Arcade mirrors its problem style. Practising in the vendor's idiom is worth more than it sounds.

Name: Codility
Notes: Another OA vendor, and their own free lessons are the best preparation for their format.

Name: CoderPad
Notes: The live-coding environment many companies conduct interviews in. Practise in the actual tool — the muscle memory matters when someone is watching.

Name: Pramp
Notes: **Free peer mock interviews.** The highest-value free item in this category: speaking practice is the skill nobody drills and every candidate fails.

Name: interviewing.io
Notes: Mock interviews with real interviewers, anonymised until the end. Paid beyond the free content.

Name: Exponent
Notes: SWE/PM/EM tracks with structured mocks. Limited free tier.

Name: Hello Interview
Notes: Currently the best free structured behavioural *and* coding prep, with a genuinely usable question bank and frameworks.

Name: Blind
Notes: The largest crowdsourced bank of real OA and interview questions, tagged by company. Treat every entry as a dated anecdote, not a syllabus. ⚠ 403s automated clients.

Name: Naukri Code360
Notes: India-centric, free, with company-tagged problem sets. A real substitute for LeetCode Premium's company filters.

Name: Coding Ninjas Studio
Notes: India-centric free problems and company-wise questions. (Their paid bootcamps are deliberately not indexed here — see Honest notes.)

Name: GeeksforGeeks company-wise
Notes: The closest free substitute for LeetCode Premium's company tags. Checklist value only — the solutions are not model answers.

Name: InterviewQuery
Notes: Data/ML-leaning interview prep; some free questions, most behind a paywall. ⚠ Rate-limits automated clients (429).

Name: takeUforward (Striver's SDE sheet)
Notes: ~190 problems, the default India placement sheet. ⚠ The site root intermittently returns 522 (Cloudflare) while deep links resolve fine.

Name: Sean Prashad — LeetCode patterns
Notes: The fastest pattern → problem map: from "I cannot solve this" to "this is a monotonic stack". A lookup table, not a course — pair it with an ordered list like NeetCode's roadmap.

Name: AlgoDaily
Notes: Daily concept review; good for maintenance, weak for depth.

Name: Structy
Notes: Pattern-based course with built-in visualisation. Paid, cheap, and unusually well-structured for absolute beginners.

Name: ByteByteGo
Notes: The best free system-design visual reference. Adjacent to DSA, but system design is the other half of the same interview loop.

Name: DataLemur
Notes: Free SQL and stats with some coding. Only relevant if you are targeting data or analytics roles.

Name: Adjacent practice platforms
Documentation: https://exercism.org/; https://exercism.org/tracks; https://www.codewars.com/; https://www.codewars.com/kata; https://adventofcode.com/; https://www.codingame.com/; https://coderbyte.com/
Notes: Language fluency (Exercism), short-kata drills (Codewars), and implementation-plus-ad-hoc-reasoning (Advent of Code). Advent of Code is the best "fun" practice there is.

Name: LeetCode official solutions
Notes: Primary when available; much of it is login-gated. Prefer it over third-party mirrors.

Name: Codeforces editorials
Notes: Written by the setters. Always prefer these to third-party write-ups — intent is not inferable from an accepted solution.

Name: AtCoder editorials
Notes: Short, precise, official, and reliably present — the best editorial culture among the big three.

Name: CodeChef Discuss
Notes: Where CodeChef editorials and the per-problem Q&A live. Search before asking; almost everything has been answered.

Name: algo.monster
Notes: Structured LeetCode-style editorials plus pattern guides. The pattern pages are the useful part.

Name: walkccc.me
Notes: The best searchable per-problem LeetCode index, with multi-language code. Fast lookup, minimal prose.

Name: leetcode.ca
Notes: Full-text searchable solutions and discussion mirror. Works without a LeetCode account.

Name: doocs/leetcode
Notes: Open source, PR-driven, actively maintained, broad language coverage. The most durable of the LeetCode repositories.

Name: neetcode.io/solutions
Notes: Consistent quality with video walkthroughs for the hard problems. Use the [roadmap](https://neetcode.io/roadmap) for ordering.

Name: Petr Mitrichev's blog
Notes: A top competitor's running analysis of every major contest, for over a decade. The best available model of how a strong contestant actually thinks.

Name: MIT OpenCourseWare
Notes: The free core of a theory CS degree. 6.006 for foundations, 6.046J/6.854J for proofs, 6.851 past CLRS-level structures, 6.042 for the discrete math that CP assumes, 18.781 for number theory.

Name: Stanford CS 97SI
Notes: "Introduction to Programming Contests" — one of very few university courses aimed straight at contests. Dense, free, and short.

Name: Stanford CS 161
Notes: Current-term design and analysis of algorithms, with notes and problem sets posted publicly.

Name: Princeton Algorithms (Coursera)
Notes: Sedgewick's course — the best-paced implementation-first algorithms course. ⚠ Coursera audit access varies by course and changes without notice.

Name: Stanford Algorithms Specialization
Notes: Roughgarden's sequence. Strengthens correctness arguments and the theory side; *Algorithms Illuminated* is the paid companion.

Name: UCSD DSA Specialization
Notes: The most practical of the three: graded coding over proofs.

Name: Discrete Mathematics Specialization
Notes: The formal backbone underneath all of the math section — logic, combinatorics, graphs.

Name: NPTEL — Design & Analysis of Algorithms (IIT Bombay)
Notes: Aligned to Indian B.Tech syllabi and GATE, free, and certifiable. The local canonical for this subject.

Name: NPTEL — DAA (CMI)
Notes: A second opinion with a CS-theory flavour; NP-completeness is done properly.

Name: SWAYAM
Notes: India's credit-bearing MOOC platform. Filter Computer Science → Algorithms / Discrete Mathematics.

Name: Harvard CS50x
Notes: Only if DSA still feels blocked by programming basics. Skip otherwise.

Name: Khan Academy
Notes: Free remediation for pre-college math gaps. Do this *before* attempting olympiad material, not alongside it.

Name: Brilliant
Notes: Paid. Builds intuition interactively; does not build contest volume.

Name: OSSU Computer Science
Notes: A full self-taught CS curriculum assembled from free university courses. Use its algorithms and discrete-math slots to sequence everything above.

Name: Course directories
Notes: Discovery mechanisms. `free-programming-books` is the canonical "what is legally free" index, with Algorithms, Competitive Programming and Mathematics sections.

Name: Commonlounge
Notes: Text-based CP and algorithms courses with a discussion layer. Beginner-friendly and occasionally stale; useful as a second explanation when the primary one does not land.

Name: CMU 15-210
Notes: Parallel and sequential data structures, with a free textbook. The best treatment of the functional/parallel DS perspective most CP resources skip.

Name: MIT 6.042 Mathematics for Computer Science
Notes: Proof techniques, induction, counting, probability. Fixes the actual deficit most CP learners have: it is not coding, it is proof and counting.

Name: Codeforces blog
Notes: The best single directory of CP resources, maintained in the open on the largest CP site. Start here when you want something this page does not list.

Name: r/competitiveprogramming
Notes: Q&A, resource threads and the endless "how do I reach X rating" archive. ⚠ Reddit 403s automated clients.

Name: r/leetcode
Notes: Interview-prep side of the community: offer timelines, OA reports, company-specific threads.

Name: r/algorithms
Notes: Smaller and more theory-leaning; good for "why does this work" questions.

Name: Errichto (video)
Notes: Contest strategy and live solving. The closest thing to watching a strong contestant think out loud.

Name: SecondThread (video)
Notes: USACO/IOI-level walkthroughs with unusually honest explanations of wrong turns.

Name: Algorithms Live! (video)
Notes: Advanced contest technique, aimed past Div1-C. Watch once you can follow the references without pausing.

Name: Tushar Roy (video)
Notes: Classic DSA explained slowly and completely. Best for first exposure to a structure.

Name: Abdul Bari (video)
Notes: Exam-oriented algorithm analysis; excellent for complexity derivations.

Name: NeetCode (video)
Notes: LeetCode pattern walkthroughs, matched to the [roadmap](https://neetcode.io/roadmap).

Name: take U forward (video)
Notes: India placement DSA, Hindi/English. Large, systematic, beginner-friendly.

Name: Algorithmist — Programming Live with Larry
Notes: The best pure "video solutions" channel: Larry was a red Topcoder, a Google Code Jam finalist, top-100 on Advent of Code and top-50 on LeetCode, and he has run 500+ interviews. He solves live and explains as *both* interviewer and interviewee — nobody else shows you both sides of that dialogue.

Name: Colin Galen
Notes: USACO Silver/Gold and Codeforces solution videos, with the reasoning left in. Best CP video resource between "I can do ABC C" and "I want Platinum".

Name: Back To Back SWE
Notes: Interview-pattern walkthroughs that spend real time on *why the obvious approach fails* before presenting the right one. The closest thing to a good mock interviewer on video.

Name: Kevin Naughton Jr.
Notes: Calm, complete LeetCode walkthroughs, one problem at a time. Good for your first pass over a new pattern, before you try it alone.

Name: CS Dojo
Notes: Beginner-friendly DSA from an ex-Google engineer. The right first exposure if arrays and recursion are still shaky — too slow past that point.

Name: mycodeschool
Notes: The classic DSA lecture series — pointers, linked lists, trees, hashing, DP — still among the clearest explanations ever recorded. The channel is dormant; treat it as an archive, not a feed.

Name: William Fiset
Notes: A complete DSA course in Java plus a dedicated graph-theory series, and the only channel whose videos and repository line up one-to-one. ⚠ The channel lives at the legacy `/channel/UC…` URL — the `@williamfiset` handle 404s.

Name: Aditya Verma
Notes: The dynamic-programming series that most Indian placement aspirants actually learn DP from, plus CP topic playlists. Slow, cumulative, and worth the hours if DP is your wall.

Name: Indian DSA & placement channels
Documentation: https://www.youtube.com/@CodeHelp; https://www.youtube.com/@ApnaCollegeOfficial; https://www.youtube.com/@PepCoding; https://www.youtube.com/@CodeNCode; https://www.youtube.com/@KunalKushwaha; https://www.youtube.com/@JennyslecturesCSIT; https://www.youtube.com/@NesoAcademy; https://www.youtube.com/@GateSmashers; https://www.youtube.com/@geeksforgeeksvideos
Notes: Where the Indian placement-prep consensus is formed — 450-question sheets, complete DSA playlists, and GATE material. Mostly Hindi or Hinglish. Apply the same rule as the aggregator sites: excellent for first exposure, verify every claim before repeating it.

Name: University & course channels
Notes: Full lecture recordings — MIT 6.006 and Stanford CS161 among them — and freeCodeCamp hosts complete multi-hour DSA courses (Fiset's data-structures course lives there). Slow, but they are the only videos here with an accompanying problem set.

Name: More contest & interview video solutions
Notes: Three competitors who post worked solutions with the reasoning intact. William Lin and Neal Wu sit at the Codeforces/ICPC end; Bo Qian is LeetCode-style but unusually rigorous about data-structure internals. Watch one, attempt the next one yourself.

Name: Algorithm concept channels
Notes: Concept-first videos for when the algorithm still feels like magic: Reducible on DP, graph algorithms and NP-completeness; 3Blue1Brown on the visual intuition behind linear algebra, calculus and Fourier methods; ByteByteGo for system-design diagrams. These teach *why*, never the implementation.

Name: Math channels (contest & intuition)
Notes: AoPS's own channel is the only official one here; Michael Penn and SyberMath work through olympiad-style problems on camera, blackpenredpen is the algebra/olympiad grind, MindYourDecisions is puzzle-shaped counting and probability, Numberphile is exposure. All are supplementary — none replaces working problems on paper.

Name: More course & lecture channels
Notes: Khan Academy for math remediation, Trefor Bazett for discrete math and linear algebra at university pace, AlgoExpert and Hello Interview for structured interview content with free samples. Paid upsells behind two of them — the free material stands on its own.

Name: More Indian DSA channels
Notes: The second tier of the Indian placement ecosystem: full DSA playlists, C++ and Java tracks, and interview series. Same caveat as the first cluster — first exposure is fine, verification is on you, and the paid bootcamps behind two of these are deliberately not indexed here.

Name: UC Berkeley CS 61B (video)
Notes: Hug's data-structures course, in Berkeley's order, with the labs. The Java-flavoured counterpart to MIT 6.006, and better paced for a first pass.

Name: DSA full-course playlist (video)
Notes: One continuous course rather than a topic lookup. Use it for momentum when the curated material above feels fragmented, and verify everything against CLRS or cp-algorithms.

Name: GeeksforGeeks DSA tutorial
Notes: Breadth-first coverage in the idiom Indian placement prep actually uses. Derivative and uneven; "last updated" dates are cosmetic. Read here, verify against cp-algorithms or CPH, never cite it.

Name: Programiz
Notes: Clean visual explanations for absolute beginners. Thin past intermediate level.

Name: TutorialsPoint
Notes: Old-school reference text, largely frozen. Check anything language-specific.

Name: W3Schools DSA
Notes: Five-minute orientation only.

Name: freeCodeCamp
Notes: Community articles — quality varies by author, but the search coverage is enormous.

Name: basecs
Notes: Illustrated, careful explainers on fundamental DS and algorithms. Excellent writing; ⚠ Medium 403s automated clients.

Name: Educative — Grokking the Coding Interview
Notes: Paid. The pattern taxonomy is what you are buying, not the code.

Name: TheAlgorithms
Notes: Algorithm libraries written to be *read*, not shipped. Ideal for seeing a clean implementation of something you have only used — but never copy from them into a contest: they optimise for clarity, not constant factors.

Name: LeetCode solution repositories
SDKs & notable repos: https://github.com/walkccc/LeetCode; https://github.com/neetcode-gh/leetcode; https://github.com/youngyangyang04/leetcode-master; https://github.com/labuladong/fucking-algorithm; https://github.com/azl397985856/leetcode; https://github.com/halfrost/LeetCode-Go; https://github.com/grandyang/leetcode; https://github.com/haoel/leetcode; https://github.com/soulmachine/leetcode; https://github.com/fishercoder1534/Leetcode
